da-2025-da-43.approach: For a hard-margin SVM the boundary is the perpendicular bisector of the shortest segment between the two classes' convex hulls. Find it geometrically, then scale $w, b$ so that the support vectors satisfy $y_i(w^\top x_i + b) = 1$; every option follows from that $w, b$.

steps.title: Closest points of the two classes
steps.body:
Class-2 is the single point $O=(0,0)$. The convex hull of Class-1 is the triangle $(2,0),(0,2),(2,2)$. Its point nearest to $O$ lies on the edge from $(2,0)$ to $(0,2)$, i.e. on the line $x_1+x_2=2$; the foot of the perpendicular from $O$ is $M=(1,1)$, at distance $\sqrt{1^2+1^2}=\sqrt2$.

$(2,2)$ is farther: $\sqrt{2^2+2^2}=2\sqrt2$.

steps.title: Maximum-margin boundary: $x_1 + x_2 = 1$
steps.body:
The hard-margin boundary is the perpendicular bisector of $OM$: normal direction $(1,1)$, passing through the midpoint $(0.5, 0.5)$:
$$x_1 + x_2 = 0.5+0.5 = 1.$$
So $w = (a, a)$ and $b = -a$ for some $a > 0$ (Class-1 on the positive side).

scene.caption: Boundary $x_1+x_2=1$ halfway between $O$ and the line $x_1+x_2=2$

steps.title: Scale to the canonical form
steps.body:
Support vectors must satisfy $y_i(w^\top x_i + b) = 1$:

- $O$ (Class-2): $-(a\cdot 0 + a\cdot 0 - a) = a = 1$.
- $(2,0)$: $a\cdot 2 + a \cdot 0 - a = a = 1$ ✓, and $(0,2)$ the same.

Hence $w = (1, 1)^\top$, $b = -1$. Check $(2,2)$: $2+2-1 = 3 > 1$, strictly outside the margin.

steps.title: Support vectors and margin
steps.body:
Points with $y_i(w^\top x_i+b)=1$ exactly: $O$, $(2,0)$, $(0,2)$ — **3 support vectors**; $(2,2)$ gives $3$, so it is not one.

Margin (width of the band between $w^\top x + b = \pm 1$):
$$\frac{2}{\lVert w \rVert} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{1^2+1^2}} = \frac{2}{\sqrt2} = \sqrt2,$$
which equals the gap $\lvert OM \rvert = \sqrt2$ found in step 1.

steps.title: Check each option
steps.body:
- (A) $w=(4,4)$, $b=1$ gives $+1$ at $O$ and $9$ at $(2,0)$ — both positive, so it does not even separate the classes. **False.**
- (B) 3 support vectors. **True.**
- (C) Margin $\sqrt2$. **True.**
- (D) The data are linearly separable and a hard-margin SVM classifies every training point correctly: accuracy is $100\%$, not $98\%$ (with 4 points, 98% is impossible anyway). **False.**

answer.value: **(B) and (C)** — 3 support vectors and margin $\sqrt2$, with $w=(1,1)^\top$, $b=-1$

optionAnalysis.reason: The canonical solution is $w=(1,1)$, $b=-1$. $w=(4,4), b=1$ puts $O$ ($+1$) and $(2,0)$ ($+9$) on the same side, so it is not even a separator.
$O$, $(2,0)$ and $(0,2)$ all satisfy $y_i(w^\top x_i+b)=1$; $(2,2)$ gives $3$.
$2/\lVert w\rVert = 2/\sqrt2 = \sqrt2$, the distance from $O$ to $(1,1)$.
Separable data + hard margin ⇒ $100\%$ training accuracy; 98% of 4 points is not even attainable.

da-2025-da-43.shortcut: Margin = distance between the classes = distance from $O$ to the line $x_1+x_2=2$ $= \frac{2}{\sqrt2} = \sqrt2$; the points on the margin are $O$, $(2,0)$, $(0,2)$. That settles B and C without solving for $w$.
pitfalls: Using the half-margin $1/\lVert w\rVert = 1/\sqrt2$ — GATE's "margin" is the full width $2/\lVert w\rVert$.
Counting $(2,2)$ as a support vector: it lies at functional distance $3$, outside the margin.
Accepting any $w$ in the right direction: SVM fixes the scale by $y_i(w^\top x_i+b)=1$ on support vectors.
da-2025-da-43.verification: Dual check: with $\alpha_O=1$, $\alpha_{(2,0)}=\alpha_{(0,2)}=\tfrac12$, $\alpha_{(2,2)}=0$: $\sum\alpha_i y_i = \tfrac12+\tfrac12-1 = 0$ and $w=\sum \alpha_i y_i x_i = \tfrac12(2,0)+\tfrac12(0,2) = (1,1)$ — all $\alpha_i\ge0$, so the KKT conditions hold.

da-2025-da-44.approach: Each $X_i$ is Bernoulli($p$). Linearity of expectation gives the mean of $\widehat p$; independence lets variances add, giving $\operatorname{Var}(\widehat p)=p(1-p)/n$.
concepts: Variance of a sum of independent variables

steps.title: Mean and variance of one toss
steps.body:
$X_i \in \{0,1\}$ with $P(X_i=1)=p$:
$$E[X_i] = 1\cdot p + 0\cdot(1-p) = p,\qquad E[X_i^2] = p,$$
$$\operatorname{Var}(X_i) = E[X_i^2]-E[X_i]^2 = p - p^2 = p(1-p).$$

steps.title: Expectation of $\widehat p$
steps.body:
$$E[\widehat p] = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n E[X_i] = \frac1n \cdot n p = p.$$
So (A) is true and (B) $p/n$ is false — $\widehat p$ is an unbiased estimator of $p$.

steps.title: Variance of $\widehat p$
steps.body:
The tosses are independent, so the variance of the sum is the sum of the variances, and a constant factor comes out squared:
$$\operatorname{Var}(\widehat p) = \frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n \operatorname{Var}(X_i) = \frac{1}{n^2}\cdot n\,p(1-p) = \frac{p(1-p)}{n}.$$
This depends on $n$ and shrinks as $n$ grows (for $0<p<1$): (C) true, (D) false.

answer.value: **(A) and (C)** — $E[\widehat p]=p$ and $\operatorname{Var}(\widehat p)=p(1-p)/n$ decreases with $n$

optionAnalysis.reason: $E[\widehat p] = \frac1n \cdot np = p$ by linearity.
Forgets that the sum has $n$ terms each with mean $p$: $\frac1n\cdot np = p$, not $p/n$.
$\operatorname{Var}(\widehat p) = p(1-p)/n$, which falls as $n$ grows.
The variance carries the factor $1/n$.

da-2025-da-44.shortcut: An average of $n$ i.i.d. variables keeps the mean and divides the variance by $n$: $E=p$, $\operatorname{Var} = p(1-p)/n$.
pitfalls: Pulling $1/n$ out of a variance as $1/n$ instead of $1/n^2$ (that would give $p(1-p)$, independent of $n$, and suggest D).
Confusing the mean of the sum ($np$) with the mean of the average ($p$).
da-2025-da-44.verification: Extreme check: $n=1$ gives $\widehat p = X_1$ with variance $p(1-p)$ ✓; as $n\to\infty$ the variance $\to 0$, consistent with the law of large numbers ($\widehat p \to p$).

da-2025-da-45.approach: Expand both squared norms: the $\lVert x\rVert^2$ terms cancel, leaving an affine function $w^\top x + b$. Then test each statement on that closed form.

steps.title: Expand each squared distance
steps.body: For any vector $\mu$: $\lVert \mu - x\rVert^2 = (\mu-x)^\top(\mu-x) = \lVert\mu\rVert^2 - 2\mu^\top x + \lVert x\rVert^2.$

steps.title: Subtract: the quadratic term cancels
steps.body:
$$f(x) = \big(\lVert\mu_{red}\rVert^2 - 2\mu_{red}^\top x + \lVert x\rVert^2\big) - \big(\lVert\mu_{green}\rVert^2 - 2\mu_{green}^\top x + \lVert x\rVert^2\big)$$
$$= 2(\mu_{green}-\mu_{red})^\top x + \big(\lVert\mu_{red}\rVert^2 - \lVert\mu_{green}\rVert^2\big).$$
So $f(x) = w^\top x + b$ with $w = 2(\mu_{green}-\mu_{red})$ and $b = \lVert\mu_{red}\rVert^2 - \lVert\mu_{green}\rVert^2$ — functions of the two means only. (B) and (C) are true; (D) is false because no $x^\top x$ (or any degree-2) term survives.

steps.title: Test option (A) at $x = 0$
steps.body:
$$f(0) = w^\top 0 + b = \lVert\mu_{red}\rVert^2 - \lVert\mu_{green}\rVert^2.$$
If $\lVert\mu_{red}\rVert < \lVert\mu_{green}\rVert$ then $f(0) < 0$, so $x=0$ is labelled **red**, not green. (A) is false — which is also obvious directly: $0$ is closer to $\mu_{red}$ since $\lVert\mu_{red}-0\rVert<\lVert\mu_{green}-0\rVert$.

optionAnalysis.reason: $f(0)=\lVert\mu_{red}\rVert^2-\lVert\mu_{green}\rVert^2<0$ under that condition, so $0$ is labelled red.
After the $\lVert x\rVert^2$ terms cancel, $f$ is linear (affine) in $x$ — a linear classifier.
$w = 2(\mu_{green}-\mu_{red})$, $b = \lVert\mu_{red}\rVert^2-\lVert\mu_{green}\rVert^2$.
Each distance is quadratic, but their difference is not: the $\lVert x\rVert^2$ terms cancel.

da-2025-da-45.shortcut: Two equal-weight squared distances always differ by an affine function, so the nearest-mean boundary is the perpendicular bisector hyperplane of $\mu_{red}\mu_{green}$.
pitfalls: Seeing squared norms and answering "quadratic" (D) without expanding.
Reading option (A) backwards: closer to $\mu_{red}$ means red.
da-2025-da-45.verification: At the midpoint $x=\tfrac12(\mu_{red}+\mu_{green})$ both distances are equal, so $f$ must be $0$: $(\mu_{green}-\mu_{red})^\top(\mu_{red}+\mu_{green}) + \lVert\mu_{red}\rVert^2-\lVert\mu_{green}\rVert^2 = \lVert\mu_{green}\rVert^2-\lVert\mu_{red}\rVert^2+\lVert\mu_{red}\rVert^2-\lVert\mu_{green}\rVert^2 = 0$ ✓.

da-2025-da-46.approach: Read off what each declared constraint guarantees: PRIMARY KEY ⇒ unique and NOT NULL; a FOREIGN KEY only restricts values to existing parent keys; an unconstrained column may be NULL. Then refute A with a legal instance.

steps.title: `Person`: aadhaar is the primary key
steps.body: A primary key is a chosen candidate key, so `aadhaar` is a candidate key of `Person` — (C) true. Entity integrity forbids NULL in a primary-key column — (D) false.

steps.title: `Customer.phone` has no constraint
steps.body: `phone CHAR(10)` carries no `NOT NULL`, `UNIQUE` or key constraint, so a row may leave it NULL — (B) true.

steps.title: `Customer.aadhaar` is only a foreign key
steps.body: The foreign key only says every non-NULL `Customer.aadhaar` must appear in `Person.aadhaar`. Nothing makes it unique: one person may register two e-mail addresses. The instance on the canvas satisfies every declared constraint (distinct `email`s, valid FK), yet two rows share the same `aadhaar`, so `aadhaar` does not identify a `Customer` tuple — (A) false.

optionAnalysis.reason: No UNIQUE/key constraint on `Customer.aadhaar`; two customers (two e-mails) can share one aadhaar. A foreign key is not a key of the referencing table.
`phone` has no NOT NULL or key constraint.
It is the declared PRIMARY KEY of `Person`, hence a candidate key.
Primary-key attributes can never be NULL.

da-2025-da-46.shortcut: Only PRIMARY KEY/UNIQUE make keys and only PRIMARY KEY/NOT NULL forbid NULLs; FOREIGN KEY does neither.
pitfalls: Treating a foreign key as a key of the referencing relation.
Thinking a foreign-key column cannot be NULL — it can (here `Customer.aadhaar` may also be NULL).
da-2025-da-46.verification: The example instance is accepted by the schema: both rows have distinct non-NULL `email`s, the shared aadhaar exists in `Person`, and one `phone` is NULL — so A fails and B holds in a concrete case.

da-2025-da-47.approach: Compute attribute closures. Since only $BC \to A$ produces $A$, every key must contain $A$ or $BC$; that pins down all candidate keys. BCNF fails as soon as one FD has a non-superkey left side.

steps.title: Closure of $A$
steps.body: $A^+$: start $\{A\}$; $A\to BCEF$ adds $B,C,E,F$; $E\to DG$ adds $D,G$. $A^+ = \{A,B,C,D,E,F,G\}$ — all 7 attributes, and $A$ is a single attribute, so $A$ is a candidate key.

steps.title: Closure of $BC$
steps.body: $BC^+$: $BC\to A$ adds $A$, then $A^+$ adds everything: $BC^+ = ABCDEFG$. Minimal? $B^+ = \{B\}$ and $C^+=\{C\}$ (no FD has $B$ or $C$ alone on the left), so $BC$ is a candidate key.

steps.title: No other candidate keys; $E$ is not a key
steps.body:
$E^+ = \{E, D, G\}$ — not all attributes, so (C) is false.

Any superkey $K$ must yield $A$ in its closure. The only FD with $A$ on the right is $BC\to A$, so $K$ contains $A$, or derives $B$ and $C$ — but $B, C$ themselves only come from $A$. Hence $K \supseteq \{A\}$ or $K \supseteq \{B,C\}$, and the candidate keys are exactly $A$ and $BC$: (B) true, (A) false.

steps.title: BCNF check
steps.body: BCNF needs every non-trivial FD $X\to Y$ to have $X$ a superkey. $A\to BCEF$ ✓ and $BC\to A$ ✓, but $E\to DG$ has $E^+ = \{D,E,G\}$, not a superkey. So $R$ is **not** in BCNF — (D) true. (It is not even in 3NF: $D, G$ are non-prime and depend transitively on the key via $E$.)

answer.value: **(B) and (D)** — keys $A$ and $BC$; $E\to DG$ violates BCNF

optionAnalysis.reason: $BC^+$ is also all of $R$ and $BC$ is minimal, so $A$ is not the only key.
$A^+ = BC^+ = ABCDEFG$, both minimal, and every key contains $A$ or $BC$.
$E^+ = DEG$, so $E$ is not even a superkey.
$E\to DG$ with $E$ not a superkey violates BCNF.

da-2025-da-47.shortcut: Attributes never on any right side must be in every key; here every attribute appears on some right side, so look at which FDs generate $A$: only $BC\to A$ ⇒ keys $A$, $BC$.
pitfalls: Taking $E$ as a key because it appears on a left side.
Missing $BC$ as a key by stopping after $A^+$.
da-2025-da-47.verification: Brute force over single attributes and pairs: only $A^+$ (singles) and $BC^+$ (pairs without $A$) are complete; e.g. $BE^+ = BDEG$, $CE^+ = CDEG$, $BD^+ = BD$ — consistent with keys $\{A\}$, $\{B,C\}$.

da-2025-da-48.approach: The three given shortest paths fix $d(a,d)=d(e,h)=d(a,h)=3$. A candidate edge cannot exist if it would create a path of length 2 between one of these pairs; test each option against that.

steps.title: What the shortest paths tell us
steps.body:
Each given shortest path has 3 edges, so in $G$:
$$d(a,d)=3,\quad d(e,h)=3,\quad d(a,h)=3.$$
Any edge that would create a path of length $\le 2$ between such a pair contradicts the given information, so it is NOT an edge of $G$.

steps.title: Edge $(b, d)$
steps.body: If $(b,d)$ existed, $a-b-d$ would be a path of length $2 < 3 = d(a,d)$. Contradiction ⇒ $(b,d)$ is **not** an edge.

steps.title: Edge $(b, h)$
steps.body: If $(b,h)$ existed, $a-b-h$ would have length $2 < 3 = d(a,h)$. ⇒ **not** an edge.

steps.title: Edge $(e, g)$
steps.body: If $(e,g)$ existed, $e-g-h$ would have length $2 < 3 = d(e,h)$. ⇒ **not** an edge.

steps.title: Edge $(b, g)$ is consistent
steps.body:
Add $(b,g)$ to the drawn edges and recompute the three distances:
- $a\to d$: through $b-g$ we reach $g$ in 2 steps, but $g$'s other neighbours are $f, h$, neither adjacent to $d$, so the best is still $3$.
- $a\to h$: $a-b-g-h$ has length $3$ — equal to $3$, not shorter.
- $e\to h$: $e$'s only neighbour is $f$, and $f-b-g-h$ is no shortcut; still $3$.

All three paths stay shortest, so $(b,g)$ may well be an edge — it cannot be declared NOT an edge.

answer.value: **(A), (C) and (D)** — $(b,d)$, $(b,h)$ and $(e,g)$ would each shorten a given shortest path

optionAnalysis.reason: $a-b-d$ would have length 2, but $d(a,d)=3$.
Adding $(b,g)$ keeps $d(a,d)=d(e,h)=d(a,h)=3$ (e.g. $a-b-g-h$ is also length 3), so it can be an edge.
$a-b-h$ would have length 2, but $d(a,h)=3$.
$e-g-h$ would have length 2, but $d(e,h)=3$.

da-2025-da-48.shortcut: An edge $(u,v)$ is ruled out exactly when it joins a vertex adjacent to one end of a length-3 shortest path to the other end (or skips a vertex on it): $b$–$d$, $b$–$h$, $e$–$g$.
pitfalls: Answering "edges not drawn" — the figure shows only a subset, so missing edges may still exist.
Rejecting $(b,g)$ because $a-b-g-h$ is another path of length 3: ties are allowed, only a *shorter* path contradicts.
da-2025-da-48.verification: For each option the contradiction (or its absence) was checked against all three given distances; only $(b,g)$ produces no path of length $\le 2$ between $a,d$ / $e,h$ / $a,h$.

da-2025-da-49.approach: Chop $[0,1]$ into $n$ equal pieces and telescope: the triangle inequality bounds $\lvert f(1)-f(0)\rvert$ by $n\cdot(1/n)^2 = 1/n$, for every $n$. This needs no differentiability and forces the difference to be $0$.

steps.title: Telescope over $n$ equal steps
steps.body:
Let $x_k = k/n$ for $k=0,1,\dots,n$. Then
$$f(1)-f(0) = \sum_{k=1}^{n}\big(f(x_k)-f(x_{k-1})\big).$$

steps.title: Bound each step
steps.body:
By the triangle inequality and the hypothesis with $x_k - x_{k-1} = 1/n$:
$$\lvert f(1)-f(0)\rvert \le \sum_{k=1}^{n}\lvert f(x_k)-f(x_{k-1})\rvert \le \sum_{k=1}^{n}\left(\frac1n\right)^2 = n\cdot\frac{1}{n^2} = \frac1n.$$

steps.title: Let $n\to\infty$
steps.body:
$\lvert f(1)-f(0)\rvert \le \frac1n$ holds for **every** positive integer $n$, so it must be $0$:
$$f(1)-f(0) = 0.$$

da-2025-da-49.shortcut: Divide by $\lvert x-y\rvert$: $\left\lvert\frac{f(x)-f(y)}{x-y}\right\rvert \le \lvert x-y\rvert \to 0$, so $f'(x)=0$ everywhere and $f$ is constant.
pitfalls: Plugging $x=1, y=0$ only: that gives $\lvert f(1)-f(0)\rvert\le 1$, which does not determine the value.
Answering 1 from that loose bound.
da-2025-da-49.verification: Derivative route: $\lvert f(x+h)-f(x)\rvert/\lvert h\rvert \le \lvert h\rvert \to 0$, so $f'\equiv 0$ and $f$ is constant (mean value theorem); hence $f(1)=f(0)$ ✓. Example: any constant function satisfies the hypothesis.

da-2025-da-50.approach: With zero-mean data, $\frac1n\sum (u^\top x^{(i)})^2 = u^\top C u$ is the variance along $u$; over unit vectors it is maximised by the top eigenvector, where it equals $\lambda_{\max}$.
concepts: Variance along a direction $u^\top C u$

steps.title: Rewrite the sum as a quadratic form
steps.body:
The mean is $\frac1n\sum x^{(i)} = 0$, so the covariance matrix is $C = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n x^{(i)}x^{(i)\top}$. Since $(u^\top x)^2 = u^\top x\,x^\top u$:
$$\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}(u^\top x^{(i)})^2 = u^\top\Big(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n x^{(i)}x^{(i)\top}\Big)u = u^\top C u.$$

steps.title: Maximum-variance direction
steps.body: For unit $u$, $u^\top C u$ (the Rayleigh quotient) is at most $\lambda_{\max}$, with equality at the corresponding eigenvector — that is the "direction of maximum variance". Then $u^\top C u = u^\top(\lambda_{\max}u) = \lambda_{\max}\,u^\top u = \lambda_{\max}$.

steps.title: Largest eigenvalue
steps.body:
$\lambda_i = 100^{2-i}$ decreases with $i$:
$$\lambda_1 = 100^{1} = 100,\quad \lambda_2 = 100^{0} = 1,\quad \lambda_3 = 100^{-1} = 0.01,\ \dots$$
So $\lambda_{\max} = \lambda_1 = 100$ and the required value is $\mathbf{100}$.

da-2025-da-50.shortcut: Variance of the data projected on the first principal component = largest eigenvalue $=100^{2-1}=100$.
pitfalls: Reading $\lambda_i=100^{2-i}$ as $100\cdot 2^{-i}$ (gives 50).
Taking $\lambda_{100}$ or the sum of all eigenvalues (total variance) instead of $\lambda_1$.
da-2025-da-50.verification: Write $u=\sum_j c_j v_j$ in the eigenbasis with $\sum c_j^2=1$: $u^\top C u = \sum_j c_j^2 \lambda_j \le \lambda_1 \sum c_j^2 = 100$, with equality only for $u=\pm v_1$ ✓.

da-2025-da-51.approach: Draws with replacement are independent with the same black-probability $p=\frac{10}{15}$, so $S_{100}\sim\text{Binomial}(100, \tfrac23)$ and $E[S_{100}] = np$ by linearity of expectation.

steps.title: Probability of black on one draw
steps.body:
The bag has $5+10 = 15$ balls, and replacement restores it before every draw, so on each draw
$$P(\text{black}) = \frac{10}{15} = \frac23.$$

steps.title: Expected count by linearity
steps.body:
Let $B_k = 1$ if draw $k$ is black. Then $S_{100} = \sum_{k=1}^{100} B_k$ and
$$E[S_{100}] = \sum_{k=1}^{100}E[B_k] = 100\times P(\text{black}) = 100\times\frac23.$$
(Equivalently $S_{100}\sim\text{Binomial}(100, \tfrac23)$, whose mean is $np$.)

steps.title: Evaluate and round
steps.body:
$$100\times\frac23 = \frac{200}{3} = 66.666\ldots$$
Rounded to one decimal place: $E[S_{100}] \approx 66.7$.

pitfalls: Using the black : white ratio $10/5 = 2$ as a probability, or the white probability $\frac{5}{15}$ (gives 33.3).
Truncating $66.67$ to $66.6$ instead of rounding (the official range accepts both 66.6 and 66.7).
da-2025-da-51.verification: Complement check: expected whites $= 100\times\frac13 = 33.3$, and $66.7+33.3=100$ draws ✓.

da-2025-da-53.approach: Trace the recursion: every argument on the way down is odd ($15 \to 7 \to 3 \to 1 \to 0$), so only the doubling branch runs; the base case returns $b=10$ and four doublings give $10\times 2^4$.

steps.title: Call chain going down
steps.body:
- $f(15,10)$: $15\%2=1$ ⇒ returns $2\cdot f(\frac{14}{2}) = 2\cdot f(7.0,10)$.
- $f(7.0,10)$: $7.0\%2 = 1.0$, and `1.0 == 1` is True ⇒ $2\cdot f(3.0,10)$.
- $f(3.0,10)$ ⇒ $2\cdot f(1.0,10)$.
- $f(1.0,10)$ ⇒ $2\cdot f(0.0,10)$.

(In Python 3 `/` gives floats, but they compare equal to the integers, so the branches are the same.)

steps.title: Base case
steps.body: $f(0.0,10)$: `0.0 == 0` is True ⇒ returns $b = 10$ (an int).

steps.title: Unwind: four doublings
steps.body:
$$f(1.0)=2\times10=20,\quad f(3.0)=2\times20=40,\quad f(7.0)=2\times40=80,\quad f(15)=2\times80=160.$$
All values are ints (the base case returns the int $10$), so the program prints **160**.

da-2025-da-53.shortcut: $15 = 1111_2$: each odd step strips a 1-bit and doubles; four 1-bits ⇒ $10\times2^4 = 160$.
pitfalls: Assuming the function multiplies, $15\times10=150$ — the odd branch doubles without adding $b$.
Worrying that `(a-1)/2` is a float: $7.0\%2 = 1.0 = 1$ and $0.0 = 0$, so the same branches run.
da-2025-da-53.verification: Closed form for this chain: $f(2^k-1, b) = 2^k b$ (induction: $f(2^k-1)=2f(2^{k-1}-1)$, $f(0)=b$). With $k=4$, $b=10$: $160$ ✓.

da-2025-da-54.approach: Simulate: the stack fills $0,1,\dots,8$; from then on each iteration pops one value, adds it to `sum`, and if it is odd also discards the next value. So only $8$ and the odd numbers $7,5,3,1$ are added.

steps.title: Push phase
steps.body: Initially $S=[0]$, $x=0$, flag $=0$. Each iteration with flag $=0$ increments $x$ and pushes it. In the iteration that pushes $8$, the test `x equals 8` sets flag $=1$, so the stack is $[0,1,2,\dots,8]$ (top $=8$) and popping starts in the same iteration.

steps.title: Pop 8 (even)
steps.body: Pop $x=8$: even, so nothing else is popped. sum $=0+8=8$. Stack $[0..7]$.

steps.title: Pop 7 (odd) and discard 6
steps.body: flag is 1, so no push. Pop $x=7$: odd ⇒ pop and discard $6$. sum $=8+7=15$. Stack $[0..5]$.

steps.title: Pop 5, 3, 1 the same way
steps.body:
- Pop $5$ (odd), discard $4$: sum $=15+5=20$, stack $[0,1,2,3]$.
- Pop $3$ (odd), discard $2$: sum $=20+3=23$, stack $[0,1]$.
- Pop $1$ (odd), discard $0$: sum $=23+1=24$, stack empty ⇒ loop ends.

da-2025-da-54.shortcut: Top is 8 (even, added); then pairs (7,6), (5,4), (3,2), (1,0) each contribute only the odd number: $8+7+5+3+1=24$.
pitfalls: Missing that the pop happens in the same iteration that pushes 8 (flag is set before the pop test).
Adding the discarded even values too (that would give $36 = 0+1+\dots+8$).
Thinking the `x equals 8` test re-triggers pushes later — it only sets flag to 1 again.
da-2025-da-54.verification: Count pops: the 9 values $0..8$ are removed as $8$, then four pairs = $1+8=9$ pops, leaving the stack empty exactly after sum reaches $24$ ✓.

da-2025-da-55.approach: With decreasing adjacency lists DFS always takes the $+2$ edge first, so it runs down the even vertices to 100, then picks up the odd vertices one per backtrack step ($99, 97, \dots, 1$). Count what comes after 50 in that order.
da-2025-da-55.given: $V=\{0,\dots,100\}$; edges $i\to i+1$ and $i\to i+2$ (when the target exists); adjacency list of $i$ is $[i+2,\ i+1]$.

steps.title: Going down the evens
steps.body: From $0$ the first neighbour is $2$, from $2$ it is $4$, … so DFS discovers $0, 2, 4, \dots, 100$ in that order without backtracking. Vertex $100$ has no out-edges ($101, 102 \notin V$).

steps.title: Backtracking picks up the odds
steps.body: Back at $98$: next neighbour $99$ is new ⇒ discover $99$. Its neighbours $100$ (and $101\notin V$) are done ⇒ back to $98$, then $96$: neighbour $97$ is new; $97\to 99, 98$ both visited. In general, returning to $2k$ discovers $2k+1$, whose targets $2k+3, 2k+2$ are already visited. So the odds are discovered in the order $99, 97, \dots, 3, 1$ (vertex $1$ last, when DFS returns to $0$).

steps.title: Count vertices after 50
steps.body:
Discovered after $50$:
- evens $52, 54, \dots, 100$: $\frac{100-52}{2}+1 = 25$
- all odds $99, \dots, 1$: $50$

Total $= 25 + 50 = 75$.

da-2025-da-55.shortcut: $101$ vertices in all; $50$ is the 26th discovered ($0,2,\dots,50$), so $101-26 = 75$ come after it.
pitfalls: Assuming DFS visits the odds on the way down (that happens with increasing adjacency lists).
Counting only the evens after 50 (25) and forgetting that every odd vertex is discovered during backtracking.
da-2025-da-55.verification: Total check: $26$ (up to and including 50) $+ 25 + 50 = 101 = \lvert V\rvert$ ✓.
